Puerto Madryn, one of the liveliest cities in northeastern Patagonia, has a population of around 80,000 and makes a striking first impression. Its beautiful waterfront overlooks the vast natural amphitheater of Golfo Nuevo. Along the promenade, you can visit one of the many restaurants serving exceptionally tasty fish and seafood. Be sure to try the famous Argentine beef and enjoy a glass of wine as well!

Puerto Madryn is a starting point for some of the most interesting excursions: a day trip to Punta Tombo, home to thousands of charming penguins from October to March; a boat trip to see Commerson's dolphins from June to March; and a visit to the Valdés Peninsula, from which a boat takes you close to remarkable southern right whales, numerous dolphins, sea lions and orcas. Southern right whales and dolphins come to these waters each year for their traditional mating rituals. Sea lions and fur seals live in the open sea relatively close to shore. They are highly active, and their spectacular leaps above the water are impressive. They are also friendly and curious: when you approach, they may swim toward you with an obvious interest in making contact. They may even seek closer contact and readily allow themselves to be stroked and visitors to play alongside them in the water. Fur seals and sea lions are known for their excellent natural navigation abilities, which let them tumble and dive, and visitors can join them in these activities. Naturally, these aquatic displays can all be filmed on camera, creating memorable footage to show friends.

In Puerto Madryn, you can book exciting excursions including a day trip to Punta Tombo, where thousands of penguins live from October to March; a boat trip to see Commerson's dolphins; and a visit to the Valdés Peninsula.

Here, the mountainous part of a journey through Peru gives way to the humid lowlands, with riverbanks, dense vegetation and boat crossings. The city serves as a departure point for trips to rainforest lodges and nature routes.

In the surrounding area, visitors discover rainforest life on walks and trips onto the water. Sightings of birds and other wildlife depend on the season, weather and luck. Excursions to Tres Chimbadas Lake and local settlements reveal different sides of the Amazon, from peaceful stretches of water to everyday life in riverside communities.

## Granite Towers and Grey Glacier: What to See in Torres del Paine, Chile

### Puerto Natales

Puerto Natales is a small town on the shores of Última Esperanza Fjord in Chilean Patagonia. The town is surrounded by mountain peaks covered in sparkling snow. Cormorants nest on the sheer cliffs along the coast, while sea lions live in burrows.

### Discover Chile's Jewel — Torres del Paine

But the most beautiful sights await in Torres del Paine National Park, a jewel of Chile with glaciers, lakes, crystal-clear rivers and waterfalls.

North of Puerto Natales lies Milodon Cave, a natural monument consisting of three caves and a rock formation. If you enjoy skiing, in winter you can also set out from here for the ski slopes of Río Turbio and the Balmaceda and Serrano glaciers.

## Discover the Beauty of the National Park

### The "Blue Towers" — Torres del Paine Park Awaits You!

The park's breathtaking mountain scenery is so magnificent that it is said to have no equal anywhere in the world and is considered one of nature's most impressive creations. The name Torres del Paine is translated from the language of the Tehuelche people as "blue towers". In 1978, UNESCO designated the park a biosphere reserve. What makes the park distinctive is that almost every landscape of Patagonia can be found here among the mountains and dozens of lakes and rivers: scrub-covered plains, humid forests, Magellanic tundra and high-altitude desert, glaciers and waterfalls.

Puerto Ordaz lies in Bolívar State and, together with San Félix, forms part of the city of Ciudad Guayana. Its location is linked to the mouth of the Caroní River, which flows into the Orinoco. The great rivers and urban development shape the character of this eastern part of Venezuela.

On journeys through the country, Puerto Ordaz serves as a transport stop between nature routes and domestic flights. Travelers return here after trips through the Gran Sabana, including routes to Mount Roraima. The city connects remote natural areas with the onward itinerary.
